 Jimmy Carr: Comedy should be taught in schools
 Entertainment 
 By PA News Agency 
 Share
 Jimmy Carr is known for hosting 8 Out Of 10 Cats and Last One Laughing UK (Ian West/PA) 
 This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today,
 and has been written by our American colleagues.
 It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald.
 Comedian Jimmy Carr has said comedy should be taught in schools.
 The 54-year-old presenter is known for hosting 8 Out Of 10 Cats and Last One Laughing UK, as well as performing his own stand-up comedy shows.
 Carr said he thinks no one is born funny and that comedy is a “teachable skill” that can help young people find their “authentic voice”.
 Jimmy Carr said comedy is a valuable skill (Matt Crossick/PA) Speaking on the High Performance podcast, he said: “I think comedy should be taught in schools, well drama more generally, but comedy specifically.
 “I think a lot of people would be drawn to it.
 “It is a teachable skill. Is it an innate ability? Are you born funny? I don’t think so.
 “I think it’s like saying you’re born able to play the piano. Yeah, people have musical ability, people might be drawn to it or have a talent for it, but I think it is something that can be taught.”
 Carr said it would be a more valuable skill than learning grade three piano.
 He added: “You will write down and order your thoughts. You’ll learn to communicate them and you will speak in your own authentic voice.
 “Is that not more valuable than grade three on the piano? I think it is because that’s a transferable skill no matter whether you do stand-up or not. Being able to present to a group and have a little bit of humour and that will help your relationships and help your job and help your presentations and everything else.
 Jimmy Carr attending the Bafta Gala 2026 at The Chancery Rosewood in central London. (Ian West/PA) “It’s a valuable skill to learn.
 “I want more people to join the choir. I want more people involved in comedy.”
 Carr went on to claim that the UK “punches way above its weight in the arts”, however he said as a country it does not lean into it as much as it should.
 The full interview can be heard on the most recent episode of the High Performance podcast.
